claims: The exact origins of April Fools' Day are uncertain.
Roman Hilaria was celebrated on March 25.
Roman Hilaria involved masquerades and practical jokes.
Medieval Festival of Fools was a week-long event leading up to April 1.
Medieval Festival of Fools involved role reversals and teasing authorities.
France adopted the Gregorian calendar under Charles IX in 1564.
France adopted the Gregorian calendar under Charles IX, moving the new year to Jan 1.
Those who kept the old tradition were mocked.
Mocked individuals sometimes had paper fish (poisson d'avril) stuck to their backs.
A popular theory links April Fools' Day to 1564, when France adopted the Gregorian calendar, moving New Year's from late March/April 1 to January 1.
Those still celebrating on April 1 were mocked as "April Fools".
Some historians suggest the April Fools' Day tradition dates back to Geoffrey Chaucer's "Canterbury Tales".
Geoffrey Chaucer's "Canterbury Tales" mentions a fox being tricked 32 days after March began.
32 days after March began is April 1.
